items.title: The Sextant: Navigating The Old Way
items.summary: Navigation is easy these days, as we’ve entire complex computerized mapping systems and radio-based positioning systems to find ourselves anywhere on Earth. It might seem simple to use GPS these days, even trivial, but billions of dollars are what it took to make that happen. Back in the day, navigation was simpler, and cheaper, using a handheld device and natural objects in space instead of artificial satellites with atomic clocks. Let’s learn about the sextant, and how it did its job. For most of human history, getting lost at sea was a very real way to die. Coastlines can be followed and landmarks recognised, but once the land drops below the horizon, a crew has little more than dead reckoning to go on. You can estimate of speed, heading and elapsed time, but errors pile up the longer you go without a concrete reference as to where you are. When land is out of sight, the sky can offer that very reference point, but you have to be able to measure it accurately enough. That’s where the sextant comes in. It’s a deceptively simple instrument that is, paradoxically, somewhat difficult to understand at a glance. It’s little more than a frame, a pair of mirrors and a small telescope, which lets a navigator measure the angle between a celestial body and the horizon to a tiny fraction of a degree. Take that measurement at the right moment, work through a few tables referencing the detected angle and the time of measurement, and you’ve got your position on the globe. The sextant was predated by the octant, which dates back to the 1730s in implementation—specifically at the hands of John Hadley and Thomas Godfrey, though Isaac Newton had described such a device in unpublished papers sometime earlier. items.title: Tiny Transmitters Track Monarch Butterflies
items.summary: Miniaturization is one thing, but how would you like to design a transmitter that attaches to a butterfly? That’s what the BlūMorpho transmitter is made to do, according to [Tom Jokinen] writing for Be Giant . Apparently, most of these butterflies have a two- to six-week life, but periodically a “super generation” spawns and lives up to nine months. This is enough time to migrate from Canada and the United States to Mexico. In Mexico, they spend the winter, and then return when the weather is more hospitable. Scientists wanted to study this migration pattern, and the tiny transmitter is exactly what they needed. You can even download an app to track the butterflies yourself. The transmitter looks like a tadpole and weighs 60 milligrams. There’s no battery, but there is a tiny solar cell. The transmitter emits a Bluetooth signal that your phone’s location services can relay. To affix the transmitter, researchers put a glassine envelope over the butterfly, weigh its wings down with something slightly heavy, and then apply eyelash glue to the transmitter. You can see the process in the video below. What else could you do with a virtually weightless Bluetooth tracker? It is possible that dedicated tracking stations could have a longer range . Impressed it’s Bluetooth, I looked into some local research on dragonflies, the transmitters they were using do very short burst transmissions that basically transmit an id, nothing else. A very tiny, very short, signal spread over a frequency such that the average receiver wouldn’t even notice the signal in the noise. With transmitters that last up to 1yr and the size of a large grain of rice, a tiny wire antenna hanging from it. No need to be alarmed, Dr. Venture, I’ll have you free in a jiffy! You’re in the hands of the Blue Morpho!

items.title: Espresso, Meet Custom-Machined Stainless Steel Boiler
items.summary: While pondering some repairs for his Gaggia Classic Pro espresso machine, [Hans Gaensbauer] ended up machining an entirely new boiler from stainless steel. It was a nontrivial undertaking, since the boiler is an assembly that integrates not only heaters and pump connections, but one end is also the group head into which the portafilter interfaces. [Hans] had to deal with machining out the contours and pockets necessary for a portafilter to lock in securely, complete with the little screen and perforated plate responsible for even water distribution. And of course, the whole thing still has to fit into the original machine. All in all, [Hans] had some constraints to work around, making it a considerably more complex job than just milling a chamber out of a block of stainless steel. Overall he matches the original as much as possible, but since the original was cast from a mold and not designed with machining in mind, the operation is a bit tricky. This is a common issue when one changes manufacturing methods: a part designed to be molded will tend to have features that prove inconvenient for machining. In the end it’s a success, complete with brand new seals and some upgraded electric components to address an original thermostat failure. If you want to see the insides of [Hans]’ espresso machine as well as loads of pictures showing the process of machining a whole new boiler and group head, check it out. items.title: A LEGO 3D Printer
items.summary: LEGO building blocks are a great toy, but every so often a hacker decides to take the little bricks outside of the toy room and make them an integral part of a build. [Adam Turaj] took that idea further than most with his Studprint, a 3D printer that’s 92% LEGO . We aren’t just talking LEGO bricks making up part of the frame here, or even the bed — though that’s obviously the case — but [Adam] goes so far that even the motion system is using LEGO leadscrews to drive the axes of this printer. Is it particularly capable? Well, no. He’s not boasting of a remarkable bed size or high speeds here because that’s really not the point. The point is that he made a printer in LEGO and if you don’t see the fun in that, we don’t know what to tell you. The whole project is open source, and includes the CAD files for the handful of non-LEGO bits you’ll need to mount the electronics, steppers and such. With an unheated bed of ABS bricks, you’re going to be limited in filament choices, but [Adam] has at least made a Benchy, which is all anyone really needs, right? In light of recent work, we can might suggest that the printer is also a pick-and-place machine . If you want to turn the phrase “LEGO 3D Printer” around, we have seen 3D Printed LEGO before as well . We’d be remiss not to note that this isn’t the first printer to use the ubiquitous building blocks we’ve seen, though this one keeps with the regular filament and extruder rather than hot glue like the 2013 version. items.title: It’s Elite, For The Commodore Pet
items.summary: A few times in the life of someone interested in technology, there comes along something which after seeing it, you know the field is never going to be the same again. For a teenage future Hackaday writer this came in seeing Elite , on a BBC Micro. Nowadays an open world game is normal, but in the mid-1980s it was mind-blowing. Of course, such a powerful piece of software couldn’t be ported to any old computer, so owners of less capable machines were left envious of their more well-heeled friends. It will be a surprise to Commodore Pet owners then, that over four decades later, [David Given] has ported the game to their platform . It’s not such a leap, as the Pet has the same (albeit slower) 6502 as the BBC Micro, and the game requires the Commodore machine to have 32k of memory. So what you get is Elite , but with the Pet’s block graphics rather than the higher-resolution you’d have seen on the newer machines. He admits it doesn’t play well and that the code is something of a mess, but we suspect 32k Pet owners in 2026 won’t be too bothered by this. All the code and disk images are there in the repository, and you can see it at work in the video below the break. items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
items.summary: This document provides a publication template and metadata structure for a technical blog post focused on building Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) using AI. It outlines key developer focus areas, product stacks, and approval workflows required for publishing technical content through Google Developer Studio. The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
items.summary: Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), BigQuery, and a four-gate defense-in-depth security stack (Model Armor, Cloud KMS, Binary Authorization, and OPA) to build governed, self-evolving AI agents that remediate live production outages in 1.8 seconds.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
items.summary: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications. This update allows developers to route long-lived, bi-directional streams and AI workloads directly through the gateway while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability. Additionally, gateways now feature deterministic default hostnames, simplifying environment provisioning and infrastructure-as-code management.

items.title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
items.summary: The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or custom enterprise stacks while retaining a unified deployment and evaluation workflow. It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Additionally, it demonstrates how platform teams can author custom extensions to enforce policies such as automated software bill of materials (SBOM) scans during deployment.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
items.summary: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12

items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
items.summary: Google AI Edge Model Explorer now supports custom compiler intermediate representations and open-source adapters like TOSA, VGF, and PTE for on-device machine learning. Developers can leverage hierarchical graph visualization, split-pane views, and per-node trace overlays to catch export regressions and verify hardware delegation. These tools enable engineering teams to transparently debug execution graphs and pinpoint cycle-level latency bottlenecks locally.
